_meta.source: Published research and official/institutional reports, each opened and quoted: IFPRI (2015), Selvaraju 2003 (Int. J. Climatol.), Naylor et al. 2002 (BIES), Roberts et al. 2009 (JAMC), FAO Dry Corridor situation report (June 2016), Limsakul 2019 (ENNRJ), Nambiappan et al. 2018 (J. Oil Palm Res., MPOB), Yuan & Yamagata 2015 (Sci. Rep.), Xue & Hill 2025 (ICES JMS).
_meta.notes: Published estimates tier: crops and countries this site's own yield fit cannot see. NOT fitted here and never to be summed with or compared as commensurate to data/enso_model.json. Each figure is transcribed from the quoted sentence; effect_low_pct/effect_high_pct are null where the source gives tonnes or no size. Rows are ordered by likely food-security impact (rank). also_fitted is true only where data/enso_outlook.json rows_all has a status 'shown' row for the same country and crop; none do. Sources checked 2026-09-24. Past-event figures are not forecasts for 2026-27; the harvest field says where an effect would land if the precedent repeats.

data.effect_text: National meher cereals −10 to −20% (1.9–3.7 Mt) in the 2015 El Niño drought
data.basis: past strong El Niño (2015), preliminary estimate
data.source_name: IFPRI blog, Dorosh & Rashid, “Ethiopia’s 2015 drought: No reason for a famine” (14 Dec 2015)
data.quote: Net cereal production from the main (2015/16 meher season) harvest currently underway may fall by 10-20 percent (1.9 to 3.7 million tons) relative to the 2014/15 harvest
data.confidence_reason: One event, preliminary woreda-level estimate by IFPRI researchers; national figure hides much larger local losses.

data.effect_text: Kharif rice about −7% (3.4 Mt) on average in El Niño years, 1950–99
data.source_name: Selvaraju, “Impact of El Niño–southern oscillation on Indian foodgrain production”, International Journal of Climatology 23
data.quote: The average drop in rice (Kharif season crop) production during a warm ENSO‐phase year was 3.4 million tonnes (7%).
data.confidence_reason: Peer-reviewed but the sample ends in 1999; irrigation has grown since, and in 2023 the final kharif rice estimate was not below the prior year.

data.effect_text: Paddy output moves about 1.4 Mt per 1 °C of August sea-surface temperature anomaly
data.basis: per °C of August Pacific SST anomaly (tonnes, not percent)
data.source_name: Naylor, Falcon, Wada & Rochberg, “Using El Niño-Southern Oscillation climate data to improve food policy planning in Indonesia”, Bulletin of Indonesian Economic Studies 38(1)
data.quote: Indonesia's paddy production varies on average by 1.4 million tons for every 1°C change in August SSTAs.
data.confidence_reason: Well-established planting-delay mechanism (area planted, not yield), so this project's yield fit cannot see it.

data.effect_text: Dry-season rice −3.7% irrigated, −13.7% rainfed per +1 °C of Jul–Sep Niño 3.4
data.source_name: Roberts et al., “El Niño–Southern Oscillation impacts on rice production in Luzon, the Philippines”, Journal of Applied Meteorology and Climatology 48(8)
data.quote: a 1°C increase in average July–September Niño-3.4 SSTA is associated with a 3.7% decrease in irrigated dry-season production but with a 13.7% decline in rainfed dry-season production.
data.confidence_reason: Peer-reviewed elasticity; Luzon only, and the paper finds no effect on the Jul–Dec crop.

data.effect_text: 82,000 t maize and 118,200 t black beans lost in the 2015 El Niño drought
data.basis: past strong El Niño (2015), ministry loss count
data.source_name: FAO, Dry Corridor Central America situation report (June 2016), citing Guatemala’s Ministry of Agriculture
data.quote: 82 000 tonnes of maize were lost, representing a total financial loss of USD 30.8 million, while 118 200 tonnes of black beans were lost
data.confidence_reason: Official loss count relayed by FAO; tonnes only, no national percentage or elasticity.

data.effect_text: Over 60% maize and 80% bean losses in Dry Corridor areas in 2015
data.basis: past strong El Niño (2015), Dry Corridor areas only, not national
data.source_name: FAO, Dry Corridor Central America situation report (June 2016)
data.quote: Preliminary estimates in the Dry Corridor indicate that crop losses are in excess of 60 percent in maize growing areas and 80 percent in bean growing areas.
data.confidence_reason: Preliminary, local (Dry Corridor) losses; national output falls far less, and there is no published elasticity.

data.effect_text: Rice output falls significantly in El Niño years; La Niña shows no matching gain
data.source_name: Limsakul, “Impacts of El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) on rice production in Thailand during 1961-2016”, Environment and Natural Resources Journal 17(4)
data.quote: Significant decline was observed only during El Niño events, highlighting a much greater influence of El Niño events on Thailand's rice production, area harvested and yield than La Niña events.
data.confidence_reason: Direction is clear and peer-reviewed, but the abstract gives no size; matters mainly through Thai rice exports.

data.effect_text: Crude palm oil −13.2% in 2016, after the 2015-16 El Niño
data.basis: past strong El Niño (2015-16), following-year output
data.harvest: 2027 output (about a year after the peak)
data.source_name: Nambiappan et al. (MPOB), “Malaysia: 100 years of resilient palm oil economic performance”, Journal of Oil Palm Research
data.quote: FFB and CPO production declined by 12.2% to 86.33 million tonnes and by 13.2% to 17.32 million tonnes respectively mainly due to the El Nino phenomena.
data.confidence_reason: One event; a 2023 study (Khor et al., Plants 12:424) finds ageing trees, not El Niño, drove the 2005–2019 yield downtrend.

data.effect_text: Wheat yield −20.8% on average in canonical El Niño years; mostly the Indian Ocean Dipole
data.basis: average of canonical El Niño years (bootstrap composite)
data.source_name: Yuan & Yamagata, “Impacts of IOD, ENSO and ENSO Modoki on the Australian winter wheat yields in recent decades”, Scientific Reports 5:17252
data.quote: In the canonical El Niño (La Niña) years, the anomaly is −20.8% (6.5%).
data.confidence_reason: The paper credits most of this to the IOD; ABARES (Sept 2026) forecasts wheat yield +18% and does not cite El Niño.

data.effect_text: Anchoveta biomass fell from 5.8 to 1.2 Mt in the 1997-98 El Niño
data.source_name: Xue & Hill, “Phenological mismatch contributes to anchoveta landings collapse under El Niño and climate change in the Peruvian upwelling system”, ICES Journal of Marine Science 82(12)
data.quote: Similarly, during the 1997–98 event, anchoveta landings declined substantially, with estimated biomass dropping sharply from 5.8 to a minimum of 1.2 million tonnes.
data.confidence_reason: Well documented fishery collapse, but anchoveta is mostly fishmeal, so the food-security effect is indirect.
